name: Software and data foundations
point: Understand enough of the surrounding software to debug the system when the model is not the problem.
topics: **Python or TypeScript:** environments, dependencies, types, async I/O, exceptions and tests. Pick one working language first.
**HTTP and APIs:** JSON, authentication, status codes, pagination, streaming, timeouts and retry semantics.
**Data work:** parsing documents, SQL, joins, schemas, provenance, deduplication and versioned datasets.
**Application structure:** a small service, persistent storage, background work, configuration and secrets.
**Git and reproducibility:** reviewable diffs, lockfiles, a repeatable run command and small test fixtures.
**Debugging:** isolate data, application, model and network failures rather than changing all four at once.
checkpoint: Take a small public document collection, parse it into a consistent schema, and make a repeatable script with one command and a test fixture.
connection: These skills support every later area. An API timeout, broken parser or incorrect join can look like a model failure.

name: Model behavior and context
point: Learn what the model sees, what you ask it to do, and how to tell whether a prompt change helped.
topics: **LLM basics:** tokens, embeddings, attention, training versus inference, context limits and probabilistic generation.
**Instructions:** task boundaries, examples, output criteria and conflicting instructions.
**Context engineering:** select evidence, order it, manage conversation state and avoid carrying irrelevant history.
**Structured outputs:** schemas, validation, refusals and incomplete responses. Valid JSON does not establish factual correctness.
**Model selection:** compare capability, quality, latency and cost on the same representative inputs.
**Memory:** separate the current context from durable user preferences, retrieved records and workflow state.
checkpoint: Compare a plain prompt, an example-based prompt and a structured-output version on the same small set of real tasks. Save failures and token usage.
connection: Prompting changes the instructions and context at inference time. Retrieval supplies evidence; fine-tuning changes model weights. They address different causes.

name: OpenAI interfaces and SDKs
point: Choose the interface according to where the application runs and who should own the agent loop.
topics: **API clients:** Python and JavaScript/TypeScript libraries for making model and platform requests.
**Responses API:** direct model integration, output events, tools, streaming and application-controlled behavior.
**Agents SDK:** an agent loop inside your application, with tools, handoffs, sessions and tracing.
**Managed Agents API:** a separate managed Codex-harness runtime; inspect current availability and execution requirements.
**Codex SDK:** programmatic use of the coding-agent runtime; this differs from a generic model client.
**ChatGPT integrations:** current plugin documentation, formerly reached through Apps SDK URLs; MCP integration and embedded UI are a separate product surface.
**Operations:** projects, service credentials, usage, budgets, rate limits, data controls and deprecation monitoring.
checkpoint: Build one structured response with an official client. Then add one tool. Explain what extra problem an agent runtime would solve before adopting one.
connection: An SDK is a code library; an API is the service contract. MCP connects capabilities; it does not choose an agent runtime for you.
related: Which OpenAI interface do I use

name: Retrieval and grounding
point: Help a model answer from the right evidence, and make that evidence inspectable.
topics: **Ingestion:** extraction, OCR where necessary, document structure, deduplication, refreshes and source permissions.
**Indexing:** chunk boundaries, metadata, embedding choices, vector indexes and keyword search.
**Retrieval:** query rewriting, metadata filters, hybrid search, reranking and context assembly.
**Grounded answers:** quotations, citations, source locations, uncertainty and abstention when evidence is missing.
**Evaluation:** retrieval relevance and coverage separately from answer correctness and citation support.
**Maintenance:** changed documents, stale indexes, deletions, access-controlled search and adversarial source text.
checkpoint: Ask ten questions whose answers live in your documents and a few whose answers do not. Inspect retrieved passages before judging generated answers.
connection: RAG means retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve evidence and supply it to the model. It can improve access to information without retraining the model.

name: Tools and MCP
point: Give a model useful capabilities while keeping real permissions and execution under application control.
topics: **Function tools:** clear schemas, argument validation, useful descriptions, results and error messages.
**Execution:** the model requests an action; trusted application code decides whether and how to execute it.
**MCP:** Model Context Protocol connects AI applications to external tools, resources and prompts through a shared contract.
**Roles and transport:** host, client and server; local and remote connections; current protocol version and lifecycle.
**Identity and authorization:** user-specific access, scoped credentials and enforcement at the service boundary.
**Reliability:** read versus write actions, idempotency, confirmation, retries, cancellation and audit trails.
**Debugging:** inspect requests and responses with MCP Inspector before involving a complex agent.
checkpoint: Expose one read-only tool over a small dataset. Test it directly, then through MCP, then through the model. Try invalid inputs and denied access.
connection: MCP standardizes the connection. Your code still supplies the domain logic, permission checks and safe execution behavior.

name: Agents and workflows
point: Decide which steps should be fixed in code and which decisions should be delegated to a model.
topics: **Workflow versus agent:** a prescribed sequence versus a loop where the model selects subsequent actions.
**Single-agent execution:** tools, state, stop conditions, budgets and recovery from tool failures.
**Orchestration:** routing, parallel tasks, handoffs and multi-agent coordination when there is an observable benefit.
**Durable work:** checkpoints, resumability, background execution, cancellation and human review.
**Context and memory:** what each step can see, what persists and how irrelevant history is removed.
**Evaluation:** task completion, tool correctness, side effects, trajectory quality and cost—not just final answer fluency.
checkpoint: Solve a task with a fixed two-step workflow first. Compare it with a bounded tool-using agent on the same tasks. Keep the simpler approach unless the agent earns its complexity.
connection: Agents combine model behavior, tools and state. More agents introduce additional coordination, latency and failure modes; they are an architectural choice.

name: Evaluation and error analysis
point: Turn “it seems good” into a repeatable account of what works, what fails and what changed.
topics: **Task definition:** desired behavior, unacceptable failures and whose judgment matters.
**Dataset design:** representative inputs, edge cases, held-out examples, provenance and leakage control.
**Error analysis:** inspect real failures, group causes and choose a change that targets one cause.
**Scoring:** deterministic assertions, expert rubrics and calibrated model judges with human checks.
**Agent and RAG evaluation:** inspect retrieved evidence, tool calls, permissions and trajectories.
**Experiment design:** compare versions on the same cases; examine subgroup failures, uncertainty, cost and latency.
**Feedback:** production incidents and user corrections become new regression cases.
checkpoint: Create a small versioned task set and a rubric. Run two implementations against it, manually inspect disagreements, and write why you would keep one.
connection: Evaluation sits around the entire build loop. A failure in retrieval needs a different fix from a permission bug, unclear task or weak model.

name: Training adaptation and distillation
point: Understand when changing a model is justified, and how to measure whether the change transfers to unseen tasks.
topics: **Training data:** collection rights, cleaning, annotation, coverage, splits, contamination and versioning.
**Supervised fine-tuning:** train on task demonstrations; learn full tuning versus parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA/PEFT.
**Distillation:** use a stronger teacher’s outputs or judgments to teach a smaller student. Validate data quality and applicable usage terms.
**Preference optimization:** preference pairs, DPO, reward modeling and reinforcement learning; these are deeper electives.
**Training mechanics:** loss curves, overfitting, checkpoints, compute, quantization and reproducible experiments.
**Deployment comparison:** compare the adapted model with the original on held-out quality, latency, cost and important subgroups.
checkpoint: Begin with a paper experiment design: identify a repeated failure, a dataset you may use, a baseline and a held-out test. Train only when the evidence and access justify it.
connection: Retrieval supplies knowledge at run time; fine-tuning changes weights. Distillation is a training strategy, not a promise that a small model will retain all teacher capabilities.

name: Multimodal and realtime systems
point: Choose the interface and timing that fit the task: documents, images, speech, video or interactive audio.
topics: **Vision and documents:** image understanding, document extraction, spatial details and grounded source locations.
**Audio:** transcription, speech generation, language handling and noisy recordings.
**Realtime interaction:** streaming audio, turn detection, interruption, tool latency and recovery.
**Image and video generation:** controllability, review, provenance and task-specific quality checks.
**Modality-specific evaluation:** transcription errors, visual extraction accuracy and whether generated media meets the actual brief.
**User experience:** consent, recording indicators, visible system state and graceful text fallback.
checkpoint: Use the same small task in text and one additional modality. Measure the new error modes and waiting time instead of treating a compelling demo as sufficient evidence.
connection: Modality cuts across the map. A voice agent still needs tools, evaluation, security and operations; it is not a replacement for those layers.

name: Production and inference
point: Make the system reliable, observable and economical under real use.
topics: **Service design:** async work, queues, timeouts, cancellation, backpressure and bounded retries.
**Performance:** time to first token, total task latency, p50/p95, caching, batching and parallel work.
**Economics:** per-task cost, token use, tool costs and quality-aware model routing.
**Observability:** traces, structured logs, model/prompt/tool versions and redacted records for debugging.
**Deployment:** reproducible builds, CI checks, rollout, rollback and deprecation monitoring.
**Open-model serving:** GPU memory, quantization, batching, vLLM/SGLang/llama.cpp and operational ownership.
**Monitoring:** failure rates, quality drift, incidents and user feedback—not only uptime.
checkpoint: Instrument one end-to-end task. Record quality, cost, first-output latency and completion time; test a tool outage and demonstrate recovery.
connection: A model benchmark is only one component of system performance. Retrieval, tools, retries and UI rendering all affect the user’s wait.

name: Security and trust boundaries
point: Keep untrusted model inputs and outputs from becoming unauthorized actions or data access.
topics: **Prompt injection:** retrieved pages, documents and tool output can contain hostile instructions.
**Authorization:** enforce who can read or change what outside the model; separate users and tenants.
**Tool isolation:** narrow permissions, sandboxing, secret handling, scoped credentials and approval for consequential actions.
**Output handling:** validate before executing commands, SQL, HTML or other generated instructions.
**Data governance:** collection rights, retention, deletion, sensitive data, logging and provider data controls.
**Abuse and robustness:** adversarial testing, unbounded tool loops, resource budgets and incident response.
checkpoint: Put a hostile instruction in a retrieved document. Show that the application preserves its permissions and that the incident appears in the trace.
connection: A prompt can express a policy; trusted services must enforce access. Guardrails help, but they do not replace authorization and isolation.

name: Product and field engineering
point: Translate a real workflow into a useful system people can understand, evaluate and adopt.
topics: **Discovery:** understand the user’s work, existing tools, constraints and the cost of mistakes.
**Scoping:** choose one measurable task, establish a baseline and agree what success means.
**Integration:** customer data, identity, existing APIs and the gap between a demo and a deployed workflow.
**Interaction design:** citations, editable outputs, progress, uncertainty, confirmation and recovery.
**Adoption:** handoffs, documentation, feedback, change management and operational ownership.
**Decision records:** what changed, why, evidence, tradeoffs and when to reconsider.
checkpoint: Write a one-page task brief, show a working example to a user, and record whether it improves their work. Separate user evidence from your own design assumptions.
connection: FDE means forward-deployed engineering: working close to users to deliver an integrated system. It draws on the whole map, not only model expertise.
